title: てある, ている and ておく
summary: ている shows a thing in a state, てある shows a state left by someone's action, and ておく sets an action up and leaves its effect in place.

blocks.text: Textbooks give you English labels for these helpers. This lesson asks what each one really does. All three sit after the **て-form** of a verb, and the choice between them depends on one thing: **who or what is behind the action**.
ている with a self-move verb

A **self-move** verb (lesson 15) such as 開く describes something that happens to the subject by itself. With ている it simply describes a **state**: the window is in the open state. Nobody is mentioned. Japanese treats the window as if it were a little living thing that is "being" open.
てある with an other-move verb

An **other-move** verb such as 開ける needs someone to do it. With **ある** the window loses its "alive" feel: it is just a thing that someone acted on, and the result is still there. The marked noun (the window) stays the main carriage of the sentence, but a hidden person caused the state.

rows: The window is open (just the state)
The window is open because someone opened it
Open the window and leave it that way

blocks.jp: 黒板に名前が書いてある。
blocks.en: A name has been written on the board (and it is there).

blocks.jp: 机の上に本が置いてある。
blocks.en: A book has been put on the desk (and sits there).

blocks.jp: 冷蔵庫にケーキが入れてある。
blocks.en: Someone has put a cake in the fridge.

blocks.text: This is also why Japanese says 「と書いてある」 for writing on an object: the words were put there by someone, and they stay.
ておく: do it and leave it in place

ておく is the active side of てある. The verb **おく** means "to place", so you carry out the action and **leave its effect in place**. Textbooks say "do in advance", and that is often true, but a future purpose is not required: you can put a jar in a cupboard just to get rid of it.

blocks.jp: 旅行の前に切符を買っておく。
blocks.en: I buy the ticket before the trip and have it ready.
I let the child go on crying (and leave it that way).

items: **自動詞 + ている**: a state, no one behind it.
**他動詞 + てある**: a state someone left behind.
**て-form + おく**: do it and leave the effect in place.
Never use ある after a self-move verb: 開いてある is wrong.

questions.instruction: Which sentence says the window is open because someone opened it?
questions.note: Other-move 開ける + ある leaves a state caused by someone.

questions.prompt: ドアが＿＿ある。 (Someone closed it and it stays closed.)
questions.note: ある needs the other-move verb 閉める in the て-form.

questions.prompt: 机の上に本が置いてある。
options: A book has been put on the desk and is there
A book is falling off the desk
I am about to put a book down
Nobody has put a book there
questions.note: 置く + てある: someone put it there and it stays.

questions.instruction: Which kind of verb goes before てある?
questions.note: てある needs someone behind the action.

questions.instruction: Tap the helper that leaves the result in place
questions.note: 書いて is the verb; ある marks the state left behind.

questions.prompt: 窓が開いている describes a state without saying who caused it.
questions.note: Self-move verb + ている is a plain state.

questions.prompt: The window of the room has been left open (by someone).
questions.note: Noun を-less state: 窓が + 開けて + ある.

questions.prompt: 旅行の前に切符を買っておく。
options: Buy the ticket beforehand and have it ready
Put a ticket down on the floor
questions.note: ておく: do it and leave the effect in place.

questions.prompt: 冷蔵庫にケーキが入れてある。
options: Someone put the cake in the fridge
The cake went in by itself
Nobody; it is a natural event
questions.note: 入れる is other-move, so a hidden person did it.
開く is self-move, so it cannot take てある.

options: Leave the child to go on crying
questions.note: 泣かせる (causative) + おく: let it happen and leave it.
